Backdoor or Manipulation? Graph Mixture of Experts Can Defend Against Various Graph Adversarial Attacks

CCS: Computing methodologies   Machine learning
Yuyuan Feng Affiliation: Xiamen University Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou) email: 30920231154331@stu.xmu.edu.cn , Bin Ma Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou) email: binma@hkust-gz.edu.cn and Enyan Dai Note: Corresponding author Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou) email: enyandai@hkust-gz.edu.cn
Received  5 June 2009
Abstract.

Extensive research has highlighted the vulnerability of graph neural networks (GNNs) to adversarial attacks, including manipulation, node injection, and the recently emerging threat of backdoor attacks. However, existing defenses typically focus on a single type of attack, lacking a unified approach to simultaneously defend against multiple threats. In this work, we leverage the flexibility of the Mixture of Experts (MoE) architecture to design a scalable and unified framework for defending against backdoor, edge manipulation, and node injection attacks. Specifically, we propose an MI-based logic diversity loss to encourage individual experts to focus on distinct neighborhood structures in their decision processes, thus ensuring a sufficient subset of experts remains unaffected under perturbations in local structures. Moreover, we introduce a robustness-aware router that identifies perturbation patterns and adaptively routes perturbed nodes to corresponding robust experts. Extensive experiments conducted under various adversarial settings demonstrate that our method consistently achieves superior robustness against multiple graph adversarial attacks. Our code is available at https://github.com/ehappymonkey/RGMoE.

Keywords: 
Graph Neural Networks, Robustness, Mixture of Experts

1. Introduction

Graphs are ubiquitous data structures in numerous domains, such as social networks (Fan et al., 2019), molecular graphs  (Mansimov et al., 2019), and finance systems  (Cheng et al., 2022). Recent years, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown great success in representation learning on graphs. The success of GNNs relies on the message-passing mechanism. With this mechanism, node representations can capture information of neighbors and graph structure, benefiting various downstream tasks (Fan et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2020; Scarselli et al., 2008).

Although promising results have been achieved, recent studies have shown that GNNs are vulnerable to adversarial attacks. In other words, the predictions of GNNs can greatly degrade or be manipulated under an unnoticeable perturbation in graphs. Based on the way how the graph data is perturbed, the adversarial attacks can be categorized into manipulation attack, node injection attack, and the recent emerging backdoor attack (Dai et al., 2024b). For instance, PRBCD (Geisler et al., 2021) can fool GNNs to give false predictions on target nodes by adding or deleting an unnoticeable amount of edges of the training graph. TDGIA (Zou et al., 2021) manages to significantly reduce the global node classification performance of GNNs by injecting a small amount of labeled fake nodes. Recently, emerging backdoor attacks such as UGBA (Dai et al., 2023b) and DPGBA (Zhang et al., 2024a) can easily control the model’s prediction by injecting specifically designed triggers (i.e., node or a subgraph) into the training graph. During inference, the attacker can make the GNN misbehave when the pre-defined trigger is present.

To address the susceptibility of GNNs to adversarial attacks, many defense methods have been proposed including adversarial training (Xu et al., 2019), graph structure denoising (Jin et al., 2020) and robust aggregation (Chen et al., 2021; Geisler et al., 2021; Jin et al., 2021). However, these defense strategies have two major limitations: (i) Incomplete coverage of attacks: Most existing methods primarily address general manipulation and node injection attacks, but recent studies show that they remain vulnerable to graph backdoor attacks (Dai et al., 2023b; Zhang et al., 2024a). Moreover, the defense against backdoor attacks is rather limited (Zhang et al., 2024a; Zhang et al., 2024b), let alone a unified framework to defend against them simultaneously. (ii) Lack of scalability: Many state-of-the-art defense methods against graph adversarial attacks, such as Pro-GNN (Jin et al., 2020) and RS-GNN (Dai et al., 2022), require dense adjacency matrix computations with a time complexity of O⁡(N2)O(N^{2}). Therefore, these methods exhibit poor scalability to large-scale graph datasets. Given the above limitations, it is essential to design a unified and scalable framework that can effectively defend manipulation attacks, node injection attacks, and backdoor attacks simultaneously.

One promising direction of defending against various perturbations is to adopt the Mixture of Experts (MoE) (Jacobs et al., 1991; Wang et al., 2023; Yuan et al., 2024) architecture. Firstly, pioneering research has been conducted to promote the diversity of graph experts (Liu et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2024) for more generalizable graph representations. Inspired by the diversity of experts in MoE, some experts could rely on features unaffected by adversarial attacks, making them naturally robust against the corresponding perturbations. As shown in Fig. 1, in a vanilla graph MoE model, around 20% experts remain unaffected by backdoor perturbations (Dai et al., 2023b) on an OGB-Arxiv graph. Similarly, we also observe that some experts are more resistant to the PRBCD (Geisler et al., 2021) edge manipulation attack. Secondly, the flexibility of the routing mechanism allows perturbed nodes to be routed to experts resistant to malicious perturbations, thereby enabling accurate predictions for attacked samples. Moreover, due to sparse routing, the robustness can be achieved without significantly increasing inference-time costs. Therefore, it is promising to learn an efficient Graph MoE with diverse experts and a robustness-aware router to effectively defend against various adversarial attacks.

Two technical challenges remain to be addressed for applying Graph MoE for defending against various adversarial attacks: (i) As Fig. 1 shows, the majority of experts still rely heavily on features influenced by adversarial perturbations. Thus, how can we further diversify decision logics of the experts to ensure sufficient number of robust experts for each conducted adversarial attack? (ii) How to learn a robustness-aware router capable of accurately routing perturbed samples to the corresponding experts resistant to the introduced perturbations? To address these challenges, we propose the Robust Graph MoE (RGMoE) to defend various adversarial attacks in a unified framework. Specifically, RGMoE incorporates a logic diversity loss to encourage individual experts to focus on different neighbor nodes in their decision process. This diversity would ensure a sufficient number of robust experts for each specific type of potential perturbation. Additionally, RGMoE trains a robustness-aware router to adaptively route each perturbed node to the corresponding expert robust to that specific perturbation. By combining the experts with diverse decision logics and the robustness-aware routing mechanism, our proposed RGMoE can effectively defend against various adversarial attacks while keeping the modest inference-time costs. Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We investigate a novel problem of defending against various adversarial attacks (i.e., backdoor, manipulation, and node injection attack) with a unified framework.

  • •

    We propose a novel RGMoE framework that integrates graph experts with diverse decision logics and a robustness-aware router to defend against various graph adversarial attacks.

  • •

    Extensive experiments against various adversarial attacks on large-scale graphs demonstrate the effectiveness of our RGMoE.

2. Preliminaries

Let 𝒢=(𝒱,ℰ,𝐗)\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E},\mathbf{X}) denote a graph, where 𝒱\mathcal{V} is the set of NN nodes, ℰ⊆𝒱×𝒱\mathcal{E}\subseteq\mathcal{V}\times\mathcal{V} is the set of edges, and 𝐗∈ℝ|𝒱|×d\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|\times d} represents the set of node features. The nodes 𝒱\mathcal{V} can be divided into: 𝒱C\mathcal{V}_{C} representing clean nodes, 𝒱P\mathcal{V}_{P} representing poisoned nodes (i.e., affected by backdoor trigger, manipulated edge, or injected nodes) and unlabeled 𝒱U\mathcal{V}_{U}. The target label for the poisoned nodes (if modified) is denoted as yty_{t}. The hidden representation of a node vv is 𝐡v\mathbf{h}_{v} and 𝒩⁡(v)\mathcal{N}(v) denotes its neighborhood nodes.

2.1. Preliminaries of Mixture of Experts and Graph Adversarial Attacks

Sparse Mixture of Experts. Sparse mixture of experts (Shazeer et al., 2017) decomposes a dense network into multiple experts {E1,E2,…,EN}\{E_{1},E_{2},\dots,E_{N}\}. During inference, only a small subset of experts is activated for each input sample. A trainable gating network fϕf_{\phi} determines the subset of experts to the activated based on the input sample. Given the input x, the gating network outputs a probability distribution over experts fϕ​(𝐱)∈ℝNf_{\phi}(\mathbf{x})\in\mathbb{R}^{N}. The output of MoE is the weighted sum of the top-KK expert predictions:

(1) y=∑k∈𝒦fϕ​(𝐱)k​Ek​(𝐱).y=\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}}f_{\phi}(\mathbf{x})_{k}E_{k}(\mathbf{x}).

where 𝒦\mathcal{K} denotes indicates the set of activated top-k expert, and fϕ​(𝐱)kf_{\phi}(\mathbf{x})_{k} denotes the gating score for the expert EkE_{k}.

Graph Adversarial Attacks. Extensive studies have shown that GNNs are vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Based on the way how the graph data is perturbed, the adversarial attacks can be categorized into manipulation attack, node injection attack, and the recent emerging backdoor attack (Dai et al., 2024b):

  • •

    Graph Backdoor Attack: In backdoor attacks, the attacker adds backdoor triggers (i.e., nodes or subgraphs) to a set of selected nodes in the original graph and labels them as target class yty_{t}. The attacked GNN model trained on the poisoned graph should classify target nodes attached with the triggers as target class and behave normally for clean nodes without triggers attached.

  • •

    Manipulation Attack: In a manipulation attack, an attacker manipulates either the graph structure or node features to decrease the accuracy on the global or locally selected test nodes.

  • •

    Node Injection Attack: Different from manipulation attacks that modifies the original graph, node injection attack aims to decrease the performance by injecting malicious nodes into the training graph.

2.2. Robustness Analysis of Graph MoE

Robustness of Individual Experts. In this subsection, we first conduct preliminary experiments to investigate the robustness of experts in a vanilla graph MoE model. We train a GraphMoE (Wang et al., 2023) consisting of a gating network and 48 GNN experts and evaluate their robustness against representative graph adversarial attacks, including the backdoor attack UGBA (Dai et al., 2023b), the manipulation attack PRBCD (Geisler et al., 2021), and the node injection attack TDGIA (Zou et al., 2021). Fig. 1 shows the performance of individual experts under backdoor attacks and edge manipulation attacks. From Fig. 1(a), we can observe that around 20% experts achieve ASR less than 20%. Similarly, a small portion of experts show significantly less performance drop under the manipulation attack in Fig. 1(b). The same trend is also observed for node injection attacks in Appendix F. These justify the potential of learning graph mixture of experts against various graph adversarial attacks.

Impacts of Diversity Regularization. Although preliminary results show that some experts exhibit robustness, the majority of experts still rely heavily on features influenced by adversarial perturbations. However, without sufficient number of robust experts, router is very likely to select the non-robust experts. Thus, we explore how existing expert diversity losses affect expert robustness. Specifically, we testify the representation diversification loss ℒE​D\mathcal{L}_{ED} proposed in (Liu et al., 2023) on OGB-Arxiv under backdoor attacks in Fig. 2(a). From the Fig. 2(a), we can observe a certain degree of improvement with the additional diversify regularization. However, many experts remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This highlights the necessity of exploring more effective approaches to diversify experts’ decision logic for robustness to various adversarial attacks. The detailed formulation of ℒE​D\mathcal{L}_{ED} and results about the robustness distribution under PRBCD and TDGIA can be found in Appendix F.

Analysis of Routing. In addition to diverse graph experts robust to different attacks, the Graph MoE requires a router selects the corresponding robust expert for each perturbed node. Otherwise, routing to non-robust experts would still produce wrong predictions. Therefore, we further analyze whether the router trained in Graph MoE can effectively select the corresponding robust experts. Fig. 2(b) visualizes the routing rate to robust experts under different attacks. Here, robust experts are defined as those with less than 20% ASR for backdoor attacks, 14% ACC drop for manipulation and 5% ACC drop for node injection attacks. From Fig. 2(b), we observe that although the diversity regularization is beneficial, very few samples (less than 20%) can be routed to robust experts with the existing router. This highlights the necessity of developing a robustness-aware routing mechanism for the overall robustness of Graph MoE.

2.3. Problem Formulation

With the preliminaries of mixture of experts in Sec. 2.1 and preliminary analysis in Sec. 2.2, the problem of learning a robust graph mixture of experts against various adversarial perturbations can be formally defined as:

Problem 1.

Given a graph 𝒢=(𝒱,ℰ,𝐗)\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E},\mathbf{X}) that may poisoned by various graph adversarial attacks 𝒜\mathcal{A} (including backdoor attacks, manipulation attacks, and node injection attacks), the robust Graph MoE aims to learn a set of diverse experts ℳ={Ei}i=1K\mathcal{M}=\{E_{i}\}_{i=1}^{K}, where there exists a corresponding subset of experts 𝒮⁡(a⁡(v))⊆ℳ\mathcal{S}(a(v))\subseteq\mathcal{M} that remain unaffected for the sample vv perturbed by an attack a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}, and a robustness-aware router fϕf_{\phi} which can route the perturbed sample a⁡(v)a(v) to the corresponding robust experts 𝒮⁡(a⁡(v))\mathcal{S}(a(v)).

3. Methodology

Our preliminary analysis in Fig. 1 reveals that training a Graph MoE can yield experts identifying different key patterns, with a subset of experts robust to specific adversarial perturbations. Additionally, the preliminary analysis in Fig. 2 indicates two challenges remain to be addressed: (i) Existing diversity loss is still limited in producing diverse experts robust to different attacks. How can we further diversify decision logics of the experts to ensure the robust experts exist for each conducted adversarial attack? (ii) How can we route perturbed samples to the corresponding robust expert who remains unaffected by the introduced perturbations?

To address these challenges, we propose a novel framework RGMoE, which is illustrated in Fig. 3. As shown in Fig. 3, to capture the decision logic of each expert, we measure the contribution of neighbor nodes to the aggregated representation of center node using the mutual information estimator. To diversify the prediction logics of experts, RGMoE applies a logic diversity loss that encourages different experts to focus on distinct neighbor nodes. This ensures the emergence of a diverse subset of robust experts, each specializing in resistance to specific perturbation patterns. Additionally, RGMoE further learns a robustness-aware router to detect the perturbation patterns within samples. Based on these identified patterns, the robustness-aware router adaptively routes each perturbed sample to the corresponding expert that exhibits robustness against that perturbation. More details of RGMoE are given in the following.

3.1. Mixture of Experts Architecture

As illustrated in Fig. 3, RGMoE introduces multiple GNN experts {E1,…,En}\{E_{1},\dots,E_{n}\} that have distinct decision logics. The robustness-aware router fϕf_{\phi} aims to identify the perturbed patterns and activate only the robust experts for each perturbed sample. In this section, we present the deployed MoE architecture in RGMoE that could achieve the above goals.

Following (Wang et al., 2023), RGMoE deploys a GraphMoE layer comprising multiple graph experts. To determine which experts to use for a given node vv, a gating function fϕf_{\phi} is employed to sparsely route the top-kk experts that are denoted as 𝒦\mathcal{K}. Formally, the representation update within the GraphMoE layer can be written as:

(2) 𝐡⁡(v)=∑k∈𝒦fϕ​(v)​Ek​(v,𝒩v),\mathbf{h}(v)=\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}}f_{\phi}(v)\text{E}_{k}(v,\mathcal{N}_{v}),

where each expert EkE_{k} denotes a graph expert ( e.g., GCN (Kipf, 2016)) using information of neighbor 𝒩v\mathcal{N}_{v} with message-passing mechanism. Since the robustness-aware router require to detect the local structural patterns perturbed by the adversarial attacks, RGMoE also uses a GNN as the gating model for router, which also takes into account both the node’s features and neighbors:

(3) fϕ​(v)=Softmax​(TopK​(Q⁡(v,𝒩v))),f_{\phi}(v)=\text{Softmax}(\text{TopK}(Q(v,\mathcal{N}_{v}))),

where QQ denotes a separate GNN that can utilize both information of the center node vv and its neighbors 𝒩v\mathcal{N}_{v}.

3.2. Diversifying Expert Decision Logics

In adversarial attacks, attackers perturb neighbors 𝒩v\mathcal{N}_{v} of center node vv through structure manipulation, node injection, or backdoor implantation during the message-passing process, thereby misleading GNN predictions. To alleviate this vulnerability, we encourage different GNN experts to focus on distinct sets of neighbor nodes, enabling a diverse subset of experts to disregard perturbed patterns. We first compute the importance of each neighbor node in the message-passing process by measuring the mutual information between neighbor nodes and the aggregated representations of the center nodes. Then, a logic diversity loss is introduced to enforce different experts to rely on distinct local neighborhoods when making predictions. Next, we provide details on how we diversify the logic of each expert.

3.2.1. Capturing Logic by Mutual Information.

To capture the decision logic of the expert’s message-passing process, we quantify how much each neighbor contributes to the target node’s representation within the message-passing in each expert. Specifically, for each expert EkE_{k} in a GraphMoE layer, let 𝐡~vk\mathbf{\tilde{h}}_{v}^{k} denote the output representation of node vv, and 𝐡uk\mathbf{h}_{u}^{k} denote the input representation of its neighbor u∈𝒩vu\in\mathcal{N}_{v} used by expert EkE_{k}, we aim to measure:

(4) Ik​(u,v)=ℐ⁡(𝐡uk,𝐡~vk),I^{k}(u,v)=\mathcal{I}(\mathbf{h}_{u}^{k};\mathbf{\tilde{h}}_{v}^{k}),

where ℐ⁡(⋅,⋅)\mathcal{I}(\cdot;\cdot) denotes mutual information between two variables. Since the mutual information quantifies how much information one variable provides about another, Ik​(u,v)I^{k}(u,v) reflects neighbor uu’s contribution to the updated representation of node vv within expert EkE_{k}. By combining the mutual information contributions of all neighbors, we obtain a decision logic vector that characterizes the message-passing pattern learned by the GNN expert:

(5) 𝐈vk=[Ik​(u1,v),Ik​(u2,v),…,Ik​(u|𝒩⁡(v)|,v)],ui∈𝒩⁡(v).\mathbf{I}_{v}^{k}=[I^{k}(u_{1},v),I^{k}(u_{2},v),\dots,I^{k}(u_{|\mathcal{N}(v)|},v)],\quad u_{i}\in\mathcal{N}(v).

Since the exact mutual information is intractable, we adopt the Jensen-Shannon divergence-based MI estimator (Nowozin et al., 2016), denoted by ℐ^ωJSD​(𝐡uk,𝐡~vk)\hat{\mathcal{I}}_{\omega}^{\text{JSD}}(\mathbf{h}_{u}^{k};\mathbf{\tilde{h}}_{v}^{k}), to approximate the MI values in Eq. 5:

(6) ℐ^ωJSD​(u,v):=𝔼ℙu,v​[−sp​(−Tω​(𝐡uk,𝐡~vk))]−𝔼ℙu×ℙv​[sp​(Tω​(𝐡uk,𝐡~vk))],\hat{\mathcal{I}}_{\omega}^{\text{JSD}}(u;v):=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{u,v}}[-\text{sp}(-T_{\omega}(\mathbf{h}_{u}^{k},\mathbf{\tilde{h}}_{v}^{k}))]-\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{u}\times\mathbb{P}_{v}}[\text{sp}(T_{\omega}(\mathbf{h}_{u}^{k},\mathbf{\tilde{h}}_{v}^{k}))],

where ℙu,v\mathbb{P}_{u,v} is the joint distribution of neighbor representations and corresponding center-node outputs, and ℙu×ℙv\mathbb{P}_{u}\times\mathbb{P}_{v} denotes the product of their marginal distributions. Here, sp denotes the softplus function. Following (Nowozin et al., 2016), We train the discriminator network by maximizing the mutation information:

(7) minωℒMI=−1|𝒱|∑v∈𝒱1|𝒩⁡(v)|∑u∈𝒩⁡(v)ℐ^ωJSD(u;v).\min_{\omega}\mathcal{L}_{\text{MI}}=-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}|}\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{N}(v)|}\sum_{u\in\mathcal{N}(v)}\hat{\mathcal{I}}_{\omega}^{\text{JSD}}(u;v).

3.2.2. Logic Diversity Loss.

After obtaining each expert’s decision logic vector 𝐈vk\mathbf{I}_{v}^{k} from Eq. 5, we further diversify these decision logics by minimizing the similarity between pairs of experts. Specifically, we define a logic diversity loss that penalizes high cosine similarity between the decision logic vectors of selected KK experts:

(8) ℒlogic=2|𝒱|​K​(K−1)​∑v∈𝒱∑i=1K−1∑j=i+1Kmax⁡(0,s⁡(𝐈vi,𝐈vj)−m),\mathcal{L}_{\text{logic}}=\frac{2}{|\mathcal{V}|K(K-1)}\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}\sum_{i=1}^{K-1}\sum_{j=i+1}^{K}\max\left(0,\;s(\mathbf{I}_{v}^{i},\mathbf{I}_{v}^{j})-m\right),

where s⁡(⋅,⋅)s(\cdot,\cdot) denotes the cosine similarity between two logic vectors, and mm is a margin hyperparameter controlling the degree of diversity among experts. Minimizing this loss encourages each expert to capture distinct local neighborhood structures, thus promoting diversity in experts’ decision logics.

3.2.3. Diverse Experts Training

. With the above MoE architecture, MI estimator in Eq. 7 and logic diversity loss in Eq. 8, we jointly train the router and experts end-to-end by optimizing:

(9) minϕ,θ,ω⁡ℒE=ℒM​o​E+ℒM​I+λ​ℒlogic,\min_{\phi,\theta,\omega}\mathcal{L}_{E}=\mathcal{L}_{MoE}+\mathcal{L}_{MI}+\lambda\mathcal{L}_{\text{logic}},

where ℒMoE\mathcal{L}_{\text{MoE}} denotes the general MoE loss denotes the general MoE loss, including the classification loss and the auxiliary load-balancing loss detailed in Appendix A, and λ\lambda is a hyperparameter controlling the strength of the logic diversity regularization.

3.3. Robustness-Aware Router Training

With the MI-based logic diversity loss, RGMoE can ensure robust experts against adversarial perturbations. A robustness-aware router is still required to route the poisoned nodes to corresponding robust experts. Intuitively, experts tend to exhibit larger disagreement on perturbed nodes, since robust experts rely on features that are unaffected by perturbations, whereas non-robust experts do not. This intuition is also empirically supported by Fig. 1, where robust experts assign significantly different prediction scores to perturbed nodes than non-robust experts. Motivated by this, we treat nodes with large expert disagreement as potential perturbed samples. For these potential perturbed nodes, we lower the router’s routing confidence toward experts giving consistent predictions, encouraging it to consider experts exhibiting significant disagreement. This enhances the participation of robust experts, whose predictions on perturbed samples typically differ from those of non-robust experts. Next, we present the details of robustness-aware router training.

3.3.1. Identification of Potential Perturbed Samples.

We identify potential perturbed nodes by measuring disagreement among experts in the final GraphMoE prediction layer. Specifically, for a GraphMoE with NN experts, let 𝐲vn∈ℝC\mathbf{y}_{v}^{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{C} represent the corresponding predictive distribution. The disagreement among experts for node vv is quantified as the prediction variance:

(10) s(v)=∑n=1NKL(𝐲vn∥𝐲~v),𝐲~v=1N∑k=1N𝐲vk,s(v)=\sum_{n=1}^{N}\text{KL}(\mathbf{y}_{v}^{n}\parallel\tilde{\mathbf{y}}_{v}),\quad\tilde{\mathbf{y}}_{v}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{N}\mathbf{y}_{v}^{k},

where 𝐲~v\tilde{\mathbf{y}}_{v} is the aggregated prediction probability yvky_{v}^{k} of the expert EkE_{k}, and KL(⋅∥⋅)\text{KL}(\cdot\parallel\cdot) denotes the Kullback-Leibler divergence. We empirically observe that perturbed nodes 𝒱P\mathcal{V}_{P} generally exhibit significantly larger expert disagreement than clean nodes 𝒱C\mathcal{V}_{C}. Therefore, we define the set of identified potential perturbed nodes 𝒱^P\hat{\mathcal{V}}_{P} as those whose prediction variance exceeds a threshold derived from the distribution of s⁡(v)s(v) over all training nodes 𝒱L∪𝒱U\mathcal{V}_{L}\cup\mathcal{V}_{U}.

(11) 𝒱^P={v∈𝒱L∪𝒱U∣s⁡(v)>μs+σs},\hat{\mathcal{V}}_{P}=\{v\in\mathcal{V}_{L}\cup\mathcal{V}_{U}\mid s(v)>\mu_{s}+\sigma_{s}\},

where μs\mu_{s} and σs\sigma_{s} denote the mean and standard deviation of s⁡(i)s(i) over all nodes.

3.3.2. Encouraging to Route to Robust Experts.

With the identified perturbed nodes 𝒱^P\hat{\mathcal{V}}_{P}, we further design an objective to route poisoned nodes to robust experts. For these nodes, whose predictions exhibit large disagreement across experts, we lower their confidence in the original prediction and encourage routing toward experts with alternative predictions, i.e., potential robust experts. To achieve this, the RGMoE adopts a soft label 𝐲~v\tilde{\mathbf{y}}_{v} that aggregates predictions from all experts in the final prediction layer:

(12) 𝐲~v=1N​∑k=1N𝐲vk,\tilde{\mathbf{y}}_{v}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{N}\mathbf{y}_{v}^{k},

This soft label lowers the router’s reliance on experts with consistent but potentially non-robust predictions, thus encouraging a diversified routing strategy that leverages robust experts for improved resilience against adversarial perturbations. Moreover, to further discourage reliance on the original prediction and increase the likelihood of routing to robust experts, we optionally refine the soft label 𝐲~v\tilde{\mathbf{y}}_{v} by applying a shrinkage factor ρc\rho_{c} (where 0<ρc≤10<\rho_{c}\leq 1) to the originally predicted class and then renormalizing:

(13) 𝐲~v​(c)=ρc​𝐲~v​(c)∑j=1Cρj​𝐲~v​(j),c∈{1,…,C}.\tilde{\mathbf{y}}_{v}(c)=\frac{\rho_{c}\tilde{\mathbf{y}}_{v}(c)}{\sum_{j=1}^{C}\rho_{j}\tilde{\mathbf{y}}_{v}(j)},\quad c\in\{1,\dots,C\}.

Here, ρc\rho_{c} controls the degree of confidence reduction toward the original predicted class, thereby promoting diversified routing to robust experts. With the above constructed soft label 𝐲~v\tilde{\mathbf{y}}_{v} for perturbed nodes 𝒱^P\hat{\mathcal{V}}_{P} and hard label 𝐲v\mathbf{y}_{v} for clean nodes 𝒱C=𝒱L∖𝒱^P\mathcal{V}_{C}=\mathcal{V}_{L}\setminus\hat{\mathcal{V}}_{P}, we train the robustness-aware router by minimizing:

(14) minϕ⁡ℒrouter=1|𝒱^P|​∑v∈𝒱^Pl⁡(𝐲^v,𝐲~v)+γ​1|𝒱C|​∑v∈𝒱Cl⁡(𝐲^v,𝐲v),\min_{\phi}\mathcal{L}_{\text{router}}=\frac{1}{|\hat{\mathcal{V}}_{P}|}\sum_{v\in\hat{\mathcal{V}}_{P}}l(\hat{\mathbf{y}}_{v},\tilde{\mathbf{y}}_{v})+\gamma\frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}_{C}|}\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}_{C}}l(\hat{\mathbf{y}}_{v},\mathbf{y}_{v}),

where 𝐲^v\hat{\mathbf{y}}_{v} denotes the final predictions from the MoE, ll denotes the cross-entropy loss, and γ\gamma controls the relative weight of routing supervision from clean nodes.

3.4. Final Objective Function

Combining the diversity loss in Eq.(8) and the training of robustness-aware router by Eq.(14), the final objective function can be formulated as:

(15) minϕ,θ,ω⁡ℒtotal=ℒE+ℒrouter.\min_{\phi,\theta,\omega}\mathcal{L}_{\text{total}}=\mathcal{L}_{E}+\mathcal{L}_{\text{router}}.

The training procedure of RGMoE is divided into two phases: we first train the graph MoE model with diverse experts using ℒE\mathcal{L}_{E} to obtain robust experts; then we fine-tune the router with ℒrouter\mathcal{L}_{\text{router}} to route the perturbed nodes to these robust experts. We present the detailed training procedure of method in Algorithm 1.

3.5. Time Complexity Analysis

In this subsection, we analyze the time complexity of RGMoE. Given a graph 𝒢={𝒱,ℰ,𝐗}\mathcal{G}=\{\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E},\mathbf{X}\}, let LL be the number of GCN layers, hh the hidden dimension, d the average node degree and NN the number of experts. In the training phase, the cost of the router is approximately O⁡(L​h​|𝒱​|d+|​𝒱|​N)O(Lh|\mathcal{V}|d+\mathcal{|V|}N) for calculating the message-passing and gating score. The cost of GNN experts is approximately O⁡(L​h​|𝒱|​d​K)O(Lh|\mathcal{V}|dK), where KK is the number of activated experts and K<NK<N. According to Eq. (6), the cost of the MI estimator (i.e., an MLP) is approximately O⁡(L​h​|𝒱|​d)O(Lh|\mathcal{V}|d) by neglecting the number of negative samples, which is a small constant. The cost of calculating the logic diversity loss is approximately O⁡(L​|𝒱|​d​K2)O(L|\mathcal{V}|dK^{2}) according to Eq. (8). When training the robustness-aware router, the process of calculating expert disagreement is O⁡(|𝒱|​N)O(|\mathcal{V}|N), which is linear to the number of experts, and the process of constructing the smooth label is
